chapter.name: India, a Home to Many
chapter.blurb: Communities who made India their home: Jews, Syriac Christians, Parsis, Arabs, Siddis, Armenians, Baha'is, Polish children and Tibetans, and the Indian values of welcome.

concepts.name: Migrants to India and the story of Indian Jews
concepts.description: Communities who came to India, and how Jews sought sanctuary, the Bene Israel and the Kochi Jews.
concepts.idea: Persecuted Jews found refuge in India and kept their faith while joining Indian society.
concepts.rule: Besides Indians who move within the country, many communities came to India from other parts of the world and settled here. Jews sought sanctuary in India in several waves because of persecution elsewhere. The Bene Israel, who settled in India and started a new life, lost their holy books but remembered their prayer that there is only one God, and grew into the largest Jewish community, over 25,000 shortly after independence. Others arrived between the 12th and 19th centuries; near Kochi the Raja granted them land free of cost 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure' and they built a synagogue. Swami Vivekananda in 1893 said he was proud that India sheltered the persecuted.
concepts.example: The Raja of Kochi granted the Jews land free of cost 'as long as the world, sun and moon endure'.

concepts.name: Syriac Christians and the Parsis
concepts.description: Syriac Christians reaching Malabar, Parsis fleeing Persia, the milk and sugar legend, Zoroastrianism and its links to Vedic thought.
concepts.idea: Syriac Christians and Parsis found freedom to worship in India and enriched its culture.
concepts.rule: From the 4th century CE some Syriac-speaking Christians were persecuted, treated as heretics under Rome and suspected of helping Rome in Persia, so they travelled east along trade routes to the Malabar coast (Kerala). The Parsis, followers of Zoroastrianism founded by Zarathushtra, worship one God, Ahura Mazda, and value choosing good over evil. After the Arabs conquered the Sassanid Empire in the 7th century they faced forced conversions, the jizya tax and destruction of fire temples, and some reached Gujarat between the 8th and 10th centuries. In the legend, Raja Jadi Rana of Sanjan showed a jug full of milk, and a Parsi wise man dissolved sugar in it without spilling; the Raja gave them a home. The sacred fire burns in Udvada. Zoroastrian and Vedic thought share cosmic order and fire worship, and Avestan and Vedic Sanskrit share word roots such as soma-haoma.
concepts.example: In the legend the sugar dissolved in milk without spilling meant the Parsis would enrich the land without harming it.

concepts.name: Arab merchants, the Siddis and the Armenians
concepts.description: Arab merchants and the Cheraman Juma Masjid, the Siddis of African origin, and the Armenians in India.
concepts.idea: Arab traders, Siddis and Armenians added new cultures to India's diversity.
concepts.rule: Arab merchants came from the 7th century and settled on the west coast in Kerala, Gujarat and Karnataka, traded spices, married local women and formed communities such as the Mappila Muslims, and helped build India's oldest mosque, the Cheraman Juma Masjid. They came as peaceful traders. The Siddis are of African origin, brought as slaves of Arab, Portuguese and British traders between the 7th and 19th centuries; some gained prominence in the 18th century in Muslim rulers' armies. Their culture fuses African and Indian traditions with African-style drumming and dance; they are a scheduled tribe. Hirabai Lobi received the Padma Shri in 2023. Armenians came from the 8th century; the earliest settlement was Agra where Akbar let them build a church. Abdul Hai was Chief Justice in Akbar's court and Lady Juliana a doctor. They settled in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai.
concepts.example: Armenian Street in George Town, Chennai, recalls their presence.

concepts.name: The Baha'i community and the Good Maharaja
concepts.description: The Baha'i faith in India, and how the Maharaja of Nawanagar sheltered Polish children.
concepts.idea: India welcomed Baha'is fleeing persecution and gave a haven to Polish orphans in the Second World War.
concepts.rule: The Baha'i religion began in mid-1800s Persia under Baha'u'llah and teaches unity among all people and harmony between religions. Iran's ruling religious leaders branded them heretics and treated them badly, so some Baha'is moved to India from the late 19th century; today most Baha'is in India are Indians. The Lotus Temple in New Delhi is a Baha'i temple. During the Second World War (1939-1945) Poland was invaded and many children were orphaned. Maharaja Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja of Nawanagar (Jamnagar) mobilised the Red Cross and rescued about a thousand Polish orphans between 1942 and 1946, giving them a safe home, food and care; thousands of Polish refugees were welcomed. The Good Maharaja Square in Warsaw honours him.

concepts.name: Tibetan refugees in India
concepts.description: Tibet's Buddhist history, the Dalai Lama's asylum in 1959, Sowa Rigpa and the settlement of Tibetans in India.
concepts.idea: Tibetans found refuge in India after 1959 and preserved their culture and medicine here.
concepts.rule: In the 7th century Tibet became a centre of Buddhism. After the destruction of Nalanda in the 12th-13th centuries many monks took Sanskrit manuscripts to Tibet. From the 15th century the Dalai Lamas gained a greater role and became rulers from the mid-17th century. After China overran Tibet from 1950, a popular uprising in Lhasa in 1959 led the 14th Dalai Lama to flee across the Himalaya and India granted him asylum; he lives in Dharamshala where the Central Tibetan Administration works as a government-in-exile. His Four Commitments are promoting human values, religious harmony, preserving Tibetan culture and reviving India's civilisational heritage. India rehabilitated refugees, provided education and created settlements and monasteries such as Bylakuppe in Karnataka. Sowa Rigpa, Tibetan medicine codified in the 8th century, is part of the AYUSH programme.
concepts.example: Men-Tsee-Khang in Dharamshala practises Tibetan medicine.

concepts.description: Values like vasudhaiva kutumbakam and atithi devo bhava, why India became a haven and Indian expatriates abroad.
concepts.idea: Indian values of inclusion made India a haven and Indians abroad live by them too.
concepts.rule: The stories show a culture of acceptance and inclusion. Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means the whole world is family, sarve bhavantu sukhinah means may all creatures be happy, and atithi devo bhava means a guest is like God. The Karaniya Metta Sutta speaks of cherishing all beings like a mother her child. Wherever a sizeable Indian community lives abroad it is seen as peaceful, law-abiding, progressive and prosperous and integrates well. India developed peaceful coexistence and acceptance of many faiths, creating a haven for the persecuted. Some who came to conquer, such as the Indo-Greeks and Kushanas, were conquered by India's culture. The idea of the fundamental unity of humankind can help the world face wars, climate change and inequality.
concepts.example: Sri Sarada Devi's last message: no one is a stranger, the whole world is your own.

questions.q: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means the whole world is ____.
questions.a: family

questions.q: Atithi devo bhava means
questions.a: a guest is like God
o: a guest is like God
the world is one
may all be happy
truth alone triumphs

questions.q: Sarve bhavantu sukhinah means
questions.a: may all creatures be happy
o: may all creatures be happy
the guest is God
the world is family
victory to the good

questions.q: Which of the following statements about India's values of welcome is NOT correct?
questions.a: The concept of vasudhaiva kutumbakam is symbolised by the sacred fire that continues to burn in Udvada
o: The concept of vasudhaiva kutumbakam is symbolised by the sacred fire that continues to burn in Udvada
Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means 'the whole world is family' and has been a practice for millennia, not just a slogan
Atithi devo bhava means 'a guest is like God'
The Karaniya Metta Sutta expresses loving-kindness, comparing it to a mother protecting her only child

questions.q: Why did India become a haven for the persecuted?
questions.a: A culture of peaceful coexistence and acceptance of many faiths
o: A culture of peaceful coexistence and acceptance of many faiths
It had no borders and so people could go anywhere
It was an empty land with no people at all
It was rich in gold and so all the world came to it

questions.q: Indians abroad are seen as a ____ and law-abiding minority.
questions.a: peaceful

questions.q: Some invaders, like the Indo-Greeks, were
questions.a: conquered by India's culture
o: conquered by India's culture
never seen again after their defeat in India
always rulers of the north-west of India
unaffected by the culture of India

questions.q: What is the chapter's lesson for today's world?
questions.a: The unity of humankind can help solve crises like wars and climate change
o: The unity of humankind can help solve crises like wars and climate change
Borders must be closed to keep out other nations
Trade should stop so that each nation is safe
Each nation should isolate itself from others

questions.q: Explain 'atithi devo bhava'.
questions.a: It means a guest is like God, so hosts should welcome guests with care and respect.

questions.q: Which value fits a school welcoming a new student from another country?
questions.a: atithi devo bhava
o: atithi devo bhava
war
isolation
rivalry

questions.q: Which fits caring for all animals and people?
questions.a: sarve bhavantu sukhinah
o: sarve bhavantu sukhinah
no value
only self care
trade

questions.q: Give an example of a community welcomed in India and one value behind the welcome.
questions.a: The Parsis were welcomed in Gujarat, reflecting the value of atithi devo bhava or vasudhaiva kutumbakam.

questions.q: What do Indian communities abroad show about Indian values?
questions.a: They are peaceful, law-abiding, progressive and prosperous and integrate well, reflecting values of coexistence and hard work.

questions.q: A classmate is excluded for being different. The value to apply is
questions.a: vasudhaiva kutumbakam
o: vasudhaiva kutumbakam
rivalry so that the class competes for a prize
isolation so that the friend is left alone
punishment so that the friend learns a lesson

questions.q: Explain how the values in this chapter can solve modern problems.
questions.a: Seeing the world as family encourages peace, sharing resources and cooperation on climate change and inequality.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say vasudhaiva kutumbakam is 'not just a slogan'?
questions.a: It has been practised for millennia
o: It has been practised for millennia
It is new and was made by the writers of the book
It is a law made by Parliament for all the states
It is a song that is sung at the school assembly

questions.q: Consider these statements about India's culture of welcome. (I) Wherever there is a sizeable community of Indians living abroad, it has generally been perceived as a peaceful, law-abiding and progressive minority. (II) People who came intending to conquer India were, in some cases, instead conquered by its diverse culture, such as the Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas. (III) India's culture of peaceful coexistence developed only after independence in 1947, before which the persecuted found no haven here. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I and II
o: Only I and II
Only III
Only II
All of these

questions.q: Explain why India's culture allowed small communities to keep their identity.
questions.a: Values of acceptance and many schools of thought let communities practise their faith while joining society without pressure.

questions.q: Is India's welcome to communities still alive today? Give examples.
questions.a: A reasoned answer with examples such as refugees, students or neighbours living peacefully.

questions.q: Compile a class manuscript entry with a story or tradition that shows welcoming guests.
questions.a: An entry describing a local story or custom with an illustration and the value it shows.
